turn_text: Yeah, good. Tell us a little bit about, I guess, the mechanisms that you'd like to use to get renewable energy more prevalent in the rural areas. Is there finances involved? You'd mentioned the grant and aid program. Is there policy involved with this as well?

There is really a variety of things that we can do. One key thing that I'm focused on is we look at the big infrastructure package that we're working on here in Washington is to support something called a Clean Electricity Standard, which would be an incentive for power companies, including rural electric co-ops and municipal power companies, to add clean energy to their to their mix. So this is something that I think is going to be really, we know that this is really popular around the country. People want to see more clean energy. The beauty of this, of course, is that you can do it without having an impact on utility prices, which is also really important to people because they
don't want

to find themselves paying more for their electricity. So I think there's just a lot we can do. Another thing that I'm working on, another policy that can make a big difference if you want to support Biofuels where Minnesota is so strong is to let's install more blender pumps around the country so that people who want to choose biofuels with a higher mix of ethanol have that choice. And of course that's good for Minnesota farmers and it's also good if you want to reduce our carbon footprint which we're able to do with renewable fuels.

We're talking once again with U.S. Senator Tina Smith from Washington. You also have, if you could talk about the, I guess the reception across the aisle, our Republicans in on this and what about the House? Does this have some momentum?
Yeah. Well, the conversation that I had and the hearing that I led with Senator Ernst earlier this week was highly bipartisan. There's a lot of bipartisan support for renewable fuels and
those

programs, and good bipartisan support for the REAP program, which helps agricultural producers install renewable energy systems. I think that's a good building block for us. Now, I have to tell you, we still work hard to get Republican support for some of the more significant policy changes that we need to take to address the climate change challenges that we're facing. And boy, we've certainly seen that in Minnesota and across the country these last few weeks with this heat wave and growing drought problem. So I think we have work to do to get stronger bipartisan support, but we have some ground that we can build from with some of these renewable fuel programs.
All right. Let's talk about consolidation within the cattle market. That's kind of a separate issue, but still rural and it's something you've been working on.

Yes, this is a significant issue for cow-calf operations in cattle producers in Minnesota and around the country. What's happening is that we have four big companies which control over 80% of the processing capacity for beef in this country. And what's happening is that the cattle producers are getting squeezed. They're getting pennies on the dollar for their for their beef. And of course, consumers we're seeing are paying more for beef at the grocery store. So I've joined up with Senator Mike Rounds, Republican from South Dakota, to call on the Justice Department to look into this and to understand what anti-competitive behavior might be happening here and what we need to do about it. This is a big issue for all cattle producers, but I'm particularly worried about the smaller and beginning farmers and the farmers of color. in Minnesota who are struggling to find smaller meat processors to process their beef. And we just don't have nearly the diversity and the resilience in our processing system that we
need.
And that's what we're going to work on. We had a great hearing about this yesterday in the Senate at committee and also very strong bipartisan interest in this.

Boy, I would think so. That's a problem that I guess, you know, as a average kind of small town person, I didn't realize that there was such an issue. There's only four meat processing companies that really dominate the market. That's alarming.

And if you think about it also, two of those companies are not even American companies. And, you know, it used to be when my grandmother was young, and when I went to go visit her, every town had a, you know, its own butchering and meat locker and people could go there to get their cows processed, get their beef cows processed, and that's just not there anymore. There's been so much concentration and consolidation, and I'm concerned, of course, about what that means for the resilience of our communities. We're working on legislation that would help to encourage and support those smaller processors, which I think would be a good thing, especially for beginning farmers, smaller farmers.
